Customer service-entrance conductors are a separate Article 230 category, typically from the service point to the service disconnect, not the utility drop or lateral itself.

distractorExplanations.a: The names are reversed: drop is overhead, lateral is underground.
distractorExplanations.b: Meter-to-panel conductors are service-entrance conductors. The buried utility run to the meter is the lateral.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops and laterals are the utility supply to the service point, not the customer’s service-entrance conductors.

prompt: A 400-A service uses two conductors in parallel per phase. What must be true of those paralleled conductors?

options.text: Same length, conductor material, size, and termination for each phase set
1/0 AWG or larger, with unequal lengths allowed if that eases the pull
Same size per phase, with mixed copper and aluminum allowed in one phase
Each phase in its own metal raceway and the grounded conductor in a fourth

explanation: Paralleled conductors (310.10) must be the same length, material, circular mil area, and insulation, and they must use the same terminating method, so they share current. 1/0 AWG is the usual minimum size, but length still must match. Mixing metals in a phase, or splitting phases into separate ferrous raceways, creates unequal impedance and inductive heating.

distractorExplanations.b: 1/0 AWG is the typical minimum, but paralleled conductors of a phase must still be the same length to share current.
distractorExplanations.c: Material must match within the paralleled set; copper and aluminum in one phase will not share current equally.
distractorExplanations.d: 300.20 requires all phase conductors and the grounded conductor of the circuit in each metal raceway.

prompt: An installer wants to land equipment on the line side of the service disconnect. Which connections does 230.82 actually permit there?

options.text: Ordinary branch circuits, if each circuit has its own overcurrent device
Listed supply-side items such as metering, certain surge devices, and permitted PV taps
Nothing except the meter enclosure; all other line-side gear is forbidden
Feeder panelboards rated at 125 percent of the service-conductor ampacity

explanation: 230.82 is a short list: cable limiters, meters and meter disconnects, instrument transformers, surge protective devices, supply-side PV connections, and similar listed items. General branch circuits and feeder panelboards connect on the load side of the service disconnect. The meter is permitted, but it is not the only permitted item.

distractorExplanations.a: General branch circuits are load-side. A local breaker does not authorize a 230.82 line-side tap.
distractorExplanations.c: 230.82 lists several permitted line-side items beyond the meter, including surge devices and certain PV connections.
distractorExplanations.d: Feeder panelboards are supplied from the load side of the service disconnect, not from 230.82.

prompt: A 120/240-V dwelling service supplies mixed 120-V lighting and 240-V equipment. What current does the grounded (neutral) service conductor carry?

options.text: Full ungrounded-conductor current even when 240-V line-to-line loads are balanced
Only the current of 240-V loads such as a range or water-heater element
Unbalanced 120-V load current, plus harmonic return from nonlinear loads
Negligible current, because the neutral is bonded to the grounding electrode

explanation: On a 120/240-V service the grounded conductor returns the unbalanced 120-V load. Line-to-line 240-V loads cancel on the neutral. Nonlinear loads can add triplen harmonic current. Bonding the neutral to the electrode at the service does not stop that load current from flowing on the grounded conductor back to the source.

distractorExplanations.a: Balanced line-to-line current cancels in the neutral; the neutral is not sized as a third ungrounded conductor for that reason.
distractorExplanations.b: Pure 240-V line-to-line loads draw no neutral current; 120-V unbalance is what the neutral carries.
distractorExplanations.d: The bonding jumper creates a fault path; it does not eliminate normal unbalanced load current on the neutral.

prompt: You are selecting the service disconnecting means for a new one-family dwelling. What is the NEC minimum rating?

options.text: 60 A, which 230.79 sets as the one-family dwelling service minimum
The arithmetic sum of every branch-circuit breaker handle in the panelboard
The kVA nameplate of the utility transformer that serves the lot
The Article 220 load, and not less than 100 A for a one-family dwelling

explanation: Service equipment must be at least the Article 220 calculated load. 230.79(C) also sets a 100 A floor for a one-family dwelling disconnect. 60 A is not that dwelling minimum. Breaker-handle totals ignore demand factors, and the utility transformer rating is not the NEC service size.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) is 100 A for a one-family dwelling. 60 A is a smaller-occupancy minimum, not this dwelling floor.
distractorExplanations.b: Article 220 applies demand factors. Adding breaker handles oversizes the service and is not the Code method.
distractorExplanations.c: The serving transformer kVA does not set the premises service rating under 230.79 or Article 220.

prompt: The serving utility marks the service point on a dwelling job. What does that demarcation determine for the electrician?

options.text: The enclosure in which the main bonding jumper must be installed
Where utility conductors and rules end and NEC premises wiring begins
The exact wall on which 230.70 requires the service disconnect to be mounted
The line beyond which the NEC no longer applies and only NFPA 70E remains

explanation: The service point is the boundary between the serving utility and the premises wiring. Utility rules govern on the supply side; the NEC governs the customer’s service-entrance conductors and equipment beyond that point. The main bonding jumper and the 230.70 disconnect location are equipment rules, not the ownership line. NFPA 70E is work-practice, not the service-point definition.

distractorExplanations.a: The main bonding jumper is installed at the service disconnect/service equipment, not automatically at the utility service point.
distractorExplanations.c: 230.70 sets disconnect location by nearest point of entrance of the service conductors, not by the painted service-point mark.
distractorExplanations.d: The NEC still applies to premises wiring past the service point. 70E covers electrical safety in the workplace, not ownership.

prompt: A feeder leaves the service equipment to a remote dwelling panelboard. How must the feeder overcurrent device relate to those feeder conductors?

options.text: It may exceed conductor ampacity freely if the feeder is shorter than 50 ft
It must protect the feeder conductors, generally not exceeding their ampacity
It can be omitted because the service main already protects every downstream feeder
It is taken from Table 250.66 using the feeder equipment grounding conductor

explanation: Feeders are protected under 240.4 and Article 215: the overcurrent device generally must not exceed the conductor ampacity after any required adjustments, with only the listed next-size-up and tap exceptions. A short run is not a blanket waiver. The service main does not replace feeder protection, and Table 250.66 is not an OCPD table.

distractorExplanations.a: Length alone is not a license to oversize the breaker; 240.21 tap rules are specific and limited, not a 50-ft free pass.
distractorExplanations.c: The service OCPD protects the service conductors. Each feeder still needs its own protection unless a true tap rule applies.
distractorExplanations.d: Table 250.66 sizes grounding electrode conductors, not feeder breakers.

prompt: A candidate says a dwelling service overcurrent device cannot exceed a “Class 160” 160-A maximum. What does the NEC actually set?

options.text: 60 A as both the minimum and the maximum for any dwelling service
160 A as the dwelling-service maximum in 230.79
No 160-A cap; 100–400 A services are common as the calculated load requires
200 A as the largest service permitted for a one-family dwelling

explanation: 230.79 sets minimum disconnect ratings (100 A for a one-family dwelling), not a 160 A ceiling. Dwelling services are routinely 100, 200, 320, or 400 A when Article 220 supports them. “Class 160” is not an NEC dwelling-service class. 60 A is not the one-family floor, and 200 A is not a Code maximum.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.79(C) is a 100 A one-family minimum, not a 60 A min-and-max for dwellings.
distractorExplanations.b: 230.79 is a minimum-rating rule. It does not create a 160 A dwelling maximum.
distractorExplanations.d: The NEC does not cap one-family services at 200 A; larger services are used when the calculated load requires them.

prompt: A one-family dwelling is being wired to a recent NEC cycle that includes 230.85. Where must the emergency disconnect be located?

options.text: Only if the service is larger than 400 A; smaller dwellings are exempt
Indoors, mounted immediately beside the interior panelboard
At multifamily buildings; one- and two-family dwellings are exempt
Outdoors, readily accessible, and identified as an emergency disconnect

explanation: 230.85 requires a readily accessible outdoor emergency disconnect for one- and two-family dwellings so first responders can de-energize the premises. It is not limited to services over 400 A, it is not an indoor-beside-the-panel rule, and the requirement targets one- and two-family dwellings rather than exempting them.

distractorExplanations.a: 230.85 applies to one- and two-family dwelling services without a 400 A threshold.
distractorExplanations.b: The emergency disconnect is an outdoor, readily accessible device, not an indoor handle next to the panel.
distractorExplanations.c: The rule is written for one- and two-family dwellings; it does not flip the scope to multifamily only.

prompt: An underground service raceway enters a dwelling below grade and turns up into the meter-main. What sealing requirement applies?

options.text: Seal the entry to limit moisture and gas, using a sealant identified for the insulation
Seal overhead masts only; underground service raceways are left open to drain
Use any expanding foam, because insulation compatibility is not a Code issue
Leave the raceway unsealed, because a seal would trap condensation in the pipe

explanation: 230.8 and 300.5(G) require sealing underground raceways where they enter buildings so moisture and gases do not migrate into equipment. The sealant must be identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation. Overhead-only sealing, random foam, and a ban on seals reverse those rules.

distractorExplanations.b: 300.5(G) is aimed at raceways entering from underground, where moisture and gas travel inside the pipe.
distractorExplanations.c: The sealant must be identified for the conductor insulation; unlisted foam can damage insulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Sealing is required to keep moist air and gases out of the equipment, not prohibited as a condensation trap.

prompt: A 120/240 V overhead service crosses a residential driveway. What vertical clearance does 230.24(B) require?

options.text: 12 ft of vertical clearance above this residential driveway
18 ft of vertical clearance, as required over a public street or alley
8 ft of vertical clearance above this residential driveway
15 ft of vertical clearance above this same residential driveway

explanation: 230.24(B) requires 12 ft of vertical clearance where overhead service conductors pass over a residential driveway and the voltage to ground does not exceed 300 V. A 120/240 V service is 120 V to ground, so the 15 ft row does not apply. Eighteen feet is the clearance over a public street, alley, or road. The roof clearance in 230.24(A) is a different rule and does not set the height over this driveway.

distractorExplanations.b: Eighteen feet is the 230.24(B) clearance over a public street, alley, or road, not over a residential driveway.
distractorExplanations.c: Eight feet is not the 230.24(B) clearance over a residential driveway. The roof rule in 230.24(A) is a different height and does not apply.
distractorExplanations.d: Fifteen feet applies in the driveway category only where voltage to ground exceeds 300 V. This 120/240 V service does not.

prompt: The only place proposed for a new dwelling service disconnect is the wall inside the bathroom. The handle would be easy to reach. Is that location permitted?

options.text: Not permitted; this service disconnect cannot be installed in a bathroom
Permitted, because a handle the occupant can reach satisfies ready access
Permitted if GFCI protection is added at this bathroom disconnect
Permitted if a listed meter-main is the enclosure mounted inside that bathroom

explanation: 230.70 requires the service disconnecting means to be readily accessible, and 230.70(A)(2) prohibits installing it in a bathroom. A reachable handle does not create a bathroom exception, GFCI protection does not create one, and a listed meter-main does not make a bathroom permitted.

distractorExplanations.b: Ready access is required by 230.70, but 230.70(A)(2) still prohibits the service disconnect in a bathroom.
distractorExplanations.c: GFCI protection covers bathroom receptacles. It does not waive 230.70(A)(2) for the service disconnect.
distractorExplanations.d: Listing the enclosure as a meter-main does not authorize a bathroom. The location itself is prohibited.

prompt: The ungrounded service-entrance conductors are 3/0 AWG copper. What size copper main bonding jumper does Table 250.102(C)(1) require?

options.text: 8 AWG copper, the row for ungrounded copper of 2 AWG or smaller
4 AWG copper, the table row for 2/0 or 3/0 AWG ungrounded copper
6 AWG copper, the row for 1 AWG or 1/0 AWG ungrounded copper
2 AWG copper, the row for ungrounded copper over 3/0 AWG through 350 kcmil

explanation: Table 250.102(C)(1) sizes the main bonding jumper from the largest ungrounded service-entrance conductor. For 2/0 or 3/0 AWG copper, that copper jumper is 4 AWG. The 8 AWG row is for 2 AWG and smaller, the 6 AWG row is for 1 AWG or 1/0 AWG, and the 2 AWG row starts only when the ungrounded copper exceeds 3/0 AWG.

distractorExplanations.a: 8 AWG copper is the Table 250.102(C)(1) row for 2 AWG and smaller ungrounded copper, not for 3/0 AWG.
distractorExplanations.c: 6 AWG copper is the row for 1 AWG or 1/0 AWG ungrounded copper. These service conductors are 3/0 AWG.
distractorExplanations.d: 2 AWG copper is the next larger row, used when ungrounded copper is over 3/0 AWG through 350 kcmil.

prompt: A one-family dwelling has a single service disconnect in an outdoor enclosure. What identification does 230.70(B) require on that disconnect?

options.text: A panel directory that names the main breaker is enough
No service-disconnect mark is required for a single disconnect
Permanently marked to identify it as a service disconnect
The factory label that the enclosure is suitable for service equipment

explanation: 230.70(B) requires each service disconnect to be permanently marked to identify it as a service disconnect. A circuit directory does not replace that mark, and having only one disconnect does not waive it. The factory label that equipment is suitable for service use does not identify the disconnect itself.

distractorExplanations.a: A directory names branch circuits. 230.70(B) still requires a permanent mark on the service disconnect itself.
distractorExplanations.b: The marking rule applies to each service disconnect, including a dwelling served by only one.
distractorExplanations.d: That factory mark is the 230.66 suitability label. 230.70(B) still requires a mark that identifies the service disconnect.

prompt: Conductors leave the service point at the weatherhead, run down the mast, and terminate in the service disconnect. What are those conductors?

options.text: Feeder conductors supplying the service equipment from the weatherhead
Branch-circuit conductors, because they end on one overcurrent device
A grounding electrode conductor run down the mast to the electrode
Service-entrance conductors from the service point to the disconnect

explanation: Service-entrance conductors run from the service point to the service disconnect. On this overhead service the service point is at the weatherhead, so the mast conductors into the disconnect are service-entrance conductors. A feeder begins on the load side of that disconnect, a branch circuit is past a final overcurrent device, and a grounding electrode conductor runs to an electrode.

distractorExplanations.a: A feeder begins on the load side of the service disconnect. These conductors are still ahead of that disconnect.
distractorExplanations.b: Landing on one device does not make them a branch circuit. They are the service-entrance conductors into the service.
distractorExplanations.c: A grounding electrode conductor runs to the grounding electrode, not from the weatherhead to the service disconnect.

prompt: A subpanel of branch-circuit breakers is proposed inside a dwelling bathroom. The service disconnect is already outdoors. Does 240.24(E) allow that subpanel?

options.text: Not permitted; these branch-circuit breakers cannot be placed in the bathroom
Permitted, because 240.24(E) applies to the service disconnect and that device is outdoors
Permitted, because branch-circuit breakers are supplementary overcurrent protection
Permitted when a locked bathroom door keeps occupants away from the breakers

explanation: 240.24(E) prohibits overcurrent devices, other than supplementary overcurrent protection, in a dwelling bathroom. Branch-circuit breakers in a subpanel are not supplementary protection. Locating the service disconnect outdoors does not waive the rule for this subpanel, and a lock on the bathroom door does not make the location acceptable.

distractorExplanations.b: 240.24(E) applies to overcurrent devices in the dwelling bathroom, not only to the service disconnect in 230.70.
distractorExplanations.c: Supplementary protection is a narrow exception. Ordinary branch-circuit breakers in a subpanel are not that exception.
distractorExplanations.d: A lock does not authorize the location. 240.24(E) still prohibits those overcurrent devices in the bathroom.

prompt: A meter-main and its service breaker are proposed in a first-floor clothes closet. May those overcurrent devices be installed there?

options.text: Permitted if the closet is lighted and the door opens to a hall
Not permitted; overcurrent devices cannot be located in a clothes closet
Permitted once the clothes rod is removed and the meter-main is surface-mounted
Permitted, because 240.24(D) is a bathroom rule and does not cover a clothes closet

explanation: 240.24(D) states that overcurrent devices shall not be located in clothes closets. A meter-main contains the service overcurrent device, so placing it in this closet is not permitted. A luminaire, an empty rod, or surface mounting does not remove the prohibition. The bathroom rule is a separate paragraph and does not redefine 240.24(D).

distractorExplanations.a: A light and a hallway door do not change 240.24(D). Overcurrent devices are still prohibited in the clothes closet.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the rod and surface-mounting the enclosure do not make a clothes closet an allowed location under 240.24(D).
distractorExplanations.d: 240.24(D) is the clothes-closet prohibition. The bathroom restriction is 240.24(E) and does not replace it.

prompt: A drawing groups six service disconnects for one service and states that every NEC edition allows that group. What determines whether those six disconnects are permitted?

options.text: Six grouped disconnects are permitted for every service under every NEC edition
Exactly one service disconnect is required for every building under every edition
Check the adopted cycle before assuming six disconnects are still allowed
As many service disconnects as the meter lugs will physically accept

explanation: 230.71 limits how many service disconnects one service may have, and that section has been revised, so six grouped disconnects cannot be assumed under every adopted cycle. The authority having jurisdiction enforces the cycle it adopted. Six are not automatically allowed, exactly one is not a universal rule for every edition, and the number of meter lugs does not set the limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Treating six as permitted in every edition ignores the revision of 230.71. The adopted cycle has to be checked.
distractorExplanations.b: A rule of exactly one disconnect for every building under every edition is not how 230.71 reads in every cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Meter-lug count is equipment geometry. It is not the 230.71 limit on service disconnects for one service.

prompt: A one-family dwelling has an Article 220 calculated service load of 180 A. The standard disconnect ratings available are 100 A, 150 A, 175 A, and 200 A. Which rating satisfies that load?

options.text: 100 A, the one-family minimum used in place of the calculated load
150 A, the standard size used when this dwelling load is under 200 A
175 A, the nearest standard rating that meets this 180 A calculated load
200 A, the standard rating that is not less than the 180 A load

explanation: The service disconnect must be rated not less than the Article 220 calculated load. A calculated load of 180 A is above both 150 A and 175 A, so the standard rating that covers it is 200 A. The 100 A value in 230.79(C) is only the minimum for a one-family dwelling. It does not replace a calculated load that is already 180 A.

distractorExplanations.a: 100 A is the 230.79(C) floor for a one-family dwelling. It does not replace a calculated load of 180 A.
distractorExplanations.b: 150 A is below the 180 A calculated load. A load under 200 A does not drop the disconnect to 150 A.
distractorExplanations.c: 175 A is the nearest standard size under the load, and it is still under 180 A. The rating that covers the load is 200 A.

prompt: One dwelling service has two grouped service disconnects in separate enclosures. How must the grounded conductor be treated at those disconnects?

options.text: Brought to each service disconnect and bonded to that enclosure
Bonded at one enclosure, with no grounded conductor at the second disconnect
Floated at both disconnects because the transformer bond is treated as enough
Bonded inside the meter and isolated from both disconnect enclosures

explanation: 250.24(C) requires the grounded conductor to be routed with the ungrounded conductors to each service disconnect and bonded to that disconnect enclosure. With two grouped disconnects, each enclosure gets the grounded conductor and its bond. Bonding only one, floating the neutral, or bonding only in the meter and isolating both disconnects leaves a service enclosure without that path.

distractorExplanations.b: Bonding only one enclosure omits the grounded conductor that 250.24(C) requires at each service disconnect.
distractorExplanations.c: A bond at the utility transformer does not float the neutral in the service disconnects. Each enclosure is bonded.
distractorExplanations.d: A meter bond does not replace the bond at each service disconnect, and both enclosures cannot be isolated.

prompt: On a 120/240 V, 3-phase, 4-wire delta service, one phase measures about 208 V to the neutral. How is that phase identified and connected?

options.text: Any phase position is acceptable for the 208 V conductor
Identified orange and connected as the B phase in the panel
Treated as 240 V to ground, so no high-leg color or phase rule applies
Marked white, because 208 V to neutral is taken to mean it is grounded

explanation: On a 120/240 V, 3-phase, 4-wire delta, the phase that measures about 208 V to the neutral is the high leg. 110.15 and 230.56 require that higher-voltage conductor to be identified orange, and 408.3(E) requires it to be connected as the B phase. It is not 240 V to ground, it is not the grounded conductor, and it is not free to land on any phase.

distractorExplanations.a: The high leg is not free to land on any phase. It is identified orange and connected as the B phase.
distractorExplanations.c: The high leg is about 208 V to neutral, not 240 V to ground, and it still has to be identified and placed as B.
distractorExplanations.d: White identifies a grounded conductor. The high leg is an ungrounded phase and is identified orange.

prompt: An ordinary one-family dwelling has a very small calculated load on its overhead service drop. The crew proposes 12 AWG copper service-drop conductors. Is that size permitted?

options.text: Permitted, because the small load is within the ampacity of 12 AWG copper
Permitted for this ordinary dwelling drop by the limited-load exception
Not permitted; service-drop conductors must be at least 8 AWG copper
Permitted when the pole-to-weatherhead span is 50 ft or less

explanation: 230.23(B) requires overhead service-drop conductors to be at least 8 AWG copper. A small calculated load does not reduce that minimum to 12 AWG on an ordinary dwelling service drop. A short pole span does not change the minimum either. The limited-load exception is not the rule that sizes this drop.

distractorExplanations.a: Load ampacity can require a larger conductor, but it cannot waive the 8 AWG copper minimum in 230.23(B).
distractorExplanations.b: The limited-load exception is not the allowance for an ordinary dwelling service drop. 12 AWG is below 8 AWG copper.
distractorExplanations.d: Span length is not a sizing exception in 230.23(B). The drop still cannot be smaller than 8 AWG copper.

prompt: An unfused disconnect at the meter is proposed as the service disconnect, and the service breaker is in a panel 30 ft down the hall. Does that arrangement meet 230.91?

options.text: Permitted, because the unfused meter switch by itself is the service disconnect
Permitted if the 30 ft run is in rigid metal conduit with no splice
Permitted when the hallway breaker is within sight and can be locked open
Not permitted; the service breaker is not integral or immediately adjacent

explanation: 230.91 requires the service overcurrent device to be an integral part of the service disconnect or located immediately adjacent to it. An unfused disconnect at the meter with the breaker 30 ft down the hall separates the overcurrent device from the disconnect. Raceway type, a lock, or calling the unfused switch a complete service disconnect does not meet that location rule.

distractorExplanations.a: An unfused switch does not include the overcurrent device that 230.91 requires to be integral or immediately adjacent.
distractorExplanations.b: Conduit and a splice-free run do not make 30 ft immediately adjacent to the service disconnect under 230.91.
distractorExplanations.c: Within sight and a lock are not the 230.91 test. The overcurrent device must be integral or immediately adjacent.

prompt: A 200 A service uses 2/0 AWG copper ungrounded conductors and a concrete-encased electrode. What size copper grounding electrode conductor does Table 250.66 require?

options.text: 4 AWG copper, sized from Table 250.66 for the 2/0 AWG copper
6 AWG copper, using the cap for a sole connection to a rod
8 AWG copper, the table row for ungrounded copper of 2 AWG or smaller
2 AWG copper, the table row for copper over 3/0 AWG through 350 kcmil

explanation: Table 250.66 sizes a 4 AWG copper grounding electrode conductor when the largest ungrounded copper service conductor is 2/0 or 3/0 AWG. The limit that a sole connection to a rod need not be larger than 6 AWG copper does not apply to this concrete-encased electrode. Eight AWG is the row for 2 AWG and smaller copper, and 2 AWG is the row for copper larger than 3/0 through 350 kcmil.

distractorExplanations.b: The 6 AWG cap is for a sole connection to a rod, pipe, or plate. This electrode is concrete-encased, so that rod limit does not set the size.
distractorExplanations.c: 8 AWG copper is the Table 250.66 row for 2 AWG and smaller ungrounded copper, not for 2/0 AWG.
distractorExplanations.d: 2 AWG copper is the row for ungrounded copper over 3/0 AWG through 350 kcmil. These conductors are 2/0 AWG.

prompt: A one-family dwelling is at grade. Where does 210.52(E)(1) require a 125 V receptacle that is readily accessible from grade?

options.text: At the front of the dwelling, with the back left optional
At the front and at the back, readily accessible from grade
At one outside corner, counted once for the front and once for the back
Indoors within 6 ft of each exterior door, with no outdoor receptacle

explanation: 210.52(E)(1) requires a one-family dwelling to have a 125 V receptacle, readily accessible from grade, at the front and at the back. A front receptacle with nothing at the back does not comply. One corner device is not a substitute for both locations, and an indoor receptacle near a door is not the outdoor outlet the section requires.

distractorExplanations.a: The front alone leaves the back without the receptacle that 210.52(E)(1) requires at both locations.
distractorExplanations.c: One corner receptacle does not provide the separate front and back outlets required by 210.52(E)(1).
distractorExplanations.d: An indoor receptacle near a door is not the grade-accessible outdoor receptacle required at the front and the back.

prompt: A 480 V MCC bucket must be racked for troubleshooting and has no incident-energy label. Before energized work, an arc-flash risk assessment is required. What does that assessment primarily establish?

options.text: Available fault current used only to upsize the service overcurrent device
Rubber insulating glove class from the shock voltage of the bus
Which lockout steps may be skipped because live work is planned
Arc-rated PPE and the arc-flash boundary for the assigned task

explanation: NFPA 70E arc-flash risk assessment uses available fault current and clearing time to estimate incident energy. That result sets the arc-flash boundary and the arc-rated PPE (or PPE category) for justified energized work. It does not size service overcurrent devices, select glove class, or waive lockout.

distractorExplanations.a: Fault current comes from a short-circuit study (NEC 110.24) to rate equipment; arc-flash analysis uses it to find incident energy, not to resize the service main.
distractorExplanations.b: Glove class is a shock-risk decision from voltage and ASTM D120; arc-flash analysis sets arc-rated clothing and the arc boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: An assessment never authorizes skipping LOTO; it only specifies PPE and boundaries when energized work is justified.

prompt: A 50 hp 480 V pump will be uncoupled for a seal change. The local disconnect is opened. What must the crew still do before anyone puts a hand in the coupling?

options.text: Apply personal locks, release stored energy, and verify residual voltage is gone
Tag the disconnect without locking because the pump coupling is already off
Jog the starter once to prove the motor cannot start, then begin the seal work
Wait thirty seconds for the field to collapse, then start work without testing

explanation: OSHA 1910.147 and NFPA 70E require isolation, personal lockout, control of stored energy (rotation, springs, capacitors), and a proven absence of voltage before contact. Uncoupling the pump does not replace locks or a zero-energy test on a 480 V motor circuit.

distractorExplanations.b: A tag without a personal lock does not prevent someone from reclosing the disconnect; uncoupling is not a substitute for LOTO.
distractorExplanations.c: Jogging can start the machine unexpectedly and is not a verification method; isolation must be proven dead, not bumped.
distractorExplanations.d: Time delay does not prove de-energization; residual voltage and stored mechanical energy must be tested and released.

prompt: A 277 V lighting contactor must stay energized for in-service voltage checks. The journeyman needs hand tools at the terminals. How must those tools be rated?

options.text: To OSHA Class 00 glove voltage, because the tool rating follows glove class
To the printed arc-flash PPE category stamped on the insulated tool handle
To ASTM F1505/IEC 60900 insulation, typically 1000 V, jackets intact
By the UL file number on the jaw, treated as the insulation voltage rating

explanation: Insulated hand tools for live work are rated under ASTM F1505 / IEC 60900, commonly 1000 V, and the insulation must be intact. Glove classes, arc-flash PPE categories, and listing file numbers are different systems and do not set the tool voltage rating.

distractorExplanations.a: Class 00 (500 V ac) is an ASTM D120 rubber-glove class, not the rating system for insulated pliers or screwdrivers.
distractorExplanations.b: PPE categories describe arc-rated clothing; they are not a voltage rating printed as a tool insulation class.
distractorExplanations.d: A UL file number identifies a listed product; it is not the 1000 V insulation rating required for live-work tools.

prompt: A helper contacts a 277 V conductor and is unresponsive on the floor. The circuit is still energized. What is the first safe action?

options.text: De-energize from a safe place, call EMS, then start CPR if the scene is safe
Grab the victim’s clothing and pull them clear of the still-live conductor
Throw water on the panel so a ground-fault current will open the breaker
Wait for the victim to regain consciousness before calling EMS or a supervisor

explanation: Rescuers must not become a second victim. Open or trip the source from a safe place, summon EMS, then begin CPR or AED use only after the scene is de-energized or the victim is clear of the circuit. Direct contact with a live victim or wetting equipment is unsafe.

distractorExplanations.b: Pulling a person who is still on an energized conductor puts the rescuer in the current path.
distractorExplanations.c: Water on energized gear creates additional shock and does not reliably clear the fault.
distractorExplanations.d: Electrical shock can stop the heart; delayed EMS and CPR worsen outcomes even if the person looks merely stunned.

prompt: A VFD-fed 40 hp motor is locked out at the disconnect. The journeyman must land a new EGC at the drive terminals. Which remaining hazard must still be controlled?

options.text: Line-side residual only; load terminals are dead as soon as the disconnect opens
Dynamic braking that makes shaft coasting impossible after the stop command
No meter check at the VFD, because the locked disconnect is proof enough
Stored energy in the DC bus capacitors until discharged and verified dead

explanation: Opening a motor disconnect isolates the line but does not instantly drain a VFD DC bus. Capacitors can hold hazardous voltage for minutes. LOTO for electronic drives includes waiting the manufacturer’s discharge time, using bleed paths if provided, and proving absence of voltage at the DC bus and motor terminals.

distractorExplanations.a: Load-side and DC-bus terminals can remain live after the disconnect opens; residual energy is not limited to the line lugs.
distractorExplanations.b: Many VFDs coast on stop; braking is not guaranteed and does not remove electrical stored energy.
distractorExplanations.c: A locked disconnect is isolation, not verification; NFPA 70E still requires an absence-of-voltage test at the work point.

prompt: A 208Y/120 V panel is locked out. Before landing new branch conductors, the journeyman must prove the meter works. What is the live-dead-live sequence?

options.text: Watch the circuit go live, then dead after switching, then live again after restore
Prove two phases dead and treat the third as dead if those two readings match
Test the meter on a known live source, prove the circuit dead, then retest live
Check the calibration sticker on the meter and skip the known-live source checks

explanation: Live-dead-live proves the instrument, not the switching history. Test on a known energized source, measure every conductor on the locked-out circuit, then retest the meter on the known live source so a failed tester cannot be mistaken for a dead circuit.

distractorExplanations.a: The sequence checks the tester before and after, not whether the panel was recently energized or restored.
distractorExplanations.b: Each ungrounded conductor and the grounded conductor must be tested; two dead phases do not prove the third.
distractorExplanations.d: A current calibration sticker does not prove the meter works at this moment; known-live checks are still required.

prompt: A Class A GFCI on a 20 A construction receptacle trips when a helper uses a wet drill. What current condition caused that trip?

options.text: An arcing signature on the ungrounded conductor, which is AFCI protection
About 4–6 mA imbalance between the hot and the grounded conductor
More than 30 mA residual current, the typical equipment GFPE level
Fault current on the equipment grounding conductor that then trips the breaker

explanation: A Class A GFCI compares current leaving on the ungrounded conductor with current returning on the grounded conductor and trips at about 4–6 mA. That personnel threshold is far below 30 mA GFPE and is not the same function as an AFCI or a overcurrent device clearing via the EGC.

distractorExplanations.a: Detecting parallel or series arcing is an AFCI function; a GFCI does not look for arc signatures.
distractorExplanations.c: 30 mA is a common equipment ground-fault (GFPE) setting; it is too high for Class A personnel protection.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaker trip via the EGC is overcurrent/ground-fault clearing of large current, not a 5 mA differential trip.

prompt: Covers are off a 480 V motor-control bus. The restricted approach boundary is marked. Who may cross it to take a voltage reading?

options.text: A qualified person using shock PPE rated for the exposed voltage
An unqualified helper if a qualified person walks beside them
Anyone in arc-rated clothing, because clothing also covers shock risk
A qualified person without shock PPE if the meter reading takes under a minute

explanation: The restricted approach boundary is a shock boundary. NFPA 70E allows only a qualified person inside it, with insulating PPE and insulated tools as the voltage requires. Escort rules apply at the limited approach boundary, not the restricted boundary, and arc-rated clothing does not replace shock protection.

distractorExplanations.b: An escort may take an unqualified person to the limited approach boundary, not across the restricted shock boundary.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc-rated clothing addresses incident energy; crossing the restricted boundary is a shock decision that needs insulated PPE.
distractorExplanations.d: Task duration does not waive shock PPE inside the restricted approach boundary.

prompt: A 25 hp 480 V motor in a mechanical room is served from an MCC two rooms away. For ordinary servicing at the motor, what does NEC 430.102 require?

options.text: A remote emergency-stop pushbutton used in place of the motor disconnecting means
No local disconnect if the MCC bucket nameplate already lists this motor ID
No motor disconnect when the controller disconnect is located in another building
A lockable disconnect in sight of the motor unless a Code exception applies

explanation: NEC 430.102(B) requires a disconnecting means in sight from the motor location, and it must be lockable. Limited exceptions exist for some industrial installations with documented safety procedures. An E-stop, a nameplate, or a remote controller disconnect does not by itself meet the in-sight motor disconnect rule.

distractorExplanations.a: An E-stop may drop a starter coil; it is not the lockable disconnecting means required at the motor.
distractorExplanations.b: Identification of the MCC bucket helps lockout but does not place a disconnect in sight of the motor.
distractorExplanations.c: Distance to the controller makes an in-sight motor disconnect more necessary, not optional.

prompt: A journeyman must replace lamps from a ladder next to an exposed 277 V lighting busway. What ladder practice is required?

options.text: An aluminum ladder kept about 3 ft from the energized busway
A wood ladder painted so cracks in the side rails cannot collect moisture
Nonconductive side rails, or stay clear of the exposed energized parts
A metal ladder bonded to the enclosure before the worker climbs

explanation: OSHA and NFPA 70E expect nonconductive ladders near exposed live parts, or else maintained clearance so the ladder cannot contact them. Conductive rails put the worker in a fault path; paint on wood hides defects; bonding a metal ladder does not make contact safe.

distractorExplanations.a: Aluminum is conductive; OSHA overhead-line clearance for up to 50 kV is 10 ft, not a 3 ft busway exception.
distractorExplanations.b: Opaque coatings on wood ladders are prohibited because they hide cracks and other defects.
distractorExplanations.d: Bonding a metal ladder still leaves the climber in the path if the rail touches 277 V parts.

prompt: An unlabeled 480 V switchgear cubicle will have covers removed for an infrared scan. Why are untreated cotton work clothes not enough?

options.text: Incident energy at 480 V can exceed cotton and needs arc-rated PPE
480 V cannot sustain an arcing fault, so voltage-rated gloves are enough
Arc flash is a concern on 13.8 kV gear and is treated as negligible at 480 V
Infrared work is non-contact, so NFPA 70E clothing rules do not apply here

explanation: Low-voltage switchgear can produce high incident energy because fault current is large and clearing times can be long. Opening doors for IR work is energized work. Untreated cotton can ignite; arc-rated clothing, face protection, and a documented risk assessment are required even at 480 V.

distractorExplanations.b: 480 V systems readily sustain arcing faults; arc flash is a major hazard at this voltage.
distractorExplanations.c: Many severe arc-flash injuries occur on 480 V equipment; voltage class alone does not make it negligible.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing covers and working near exposed buses is energized work; non-contact IR does not waive 70E PPE.

prompt: A shock victim has a charred fingertip and a matching mark at the opposite boot. What do those paired marks indicate?

options.text: Surface-only burns, so internal tissue along the current path is uninjured
Current traveled through the body and damaged tissue along that path
Arc-flash radiant burns, which usually lack paired electrical contact wounds
A clothing static discharge that can closely mimic true electrical contact burns

explanation: Entry and exit burns mark where current entered and left the body. Damage along the path can include muscle, nerve, and heart injury that looks mild at the skin. That pattern is contact current, not purely radiant arc-flash burn or static.

distractorExplanations.a: Skin marks often hide deeper necrosis and cardiac effects; they are not proof the injury is superficial.
distractorExplanations.c: Arc-flash thermal burns can be extensive on exposed skin without classic entry/exit contact pairs.
distractorExplanations.d: Static discharge does not produce paired electrical contact burns of this kind.

prompt: Spare lumber and cardboard are stacked in front of a 480 V switchboard, leaving a walkway. What is wrong with that storage?

options.text: Storage is allowed if a 24 in. aisle remains in front of the switchboard
Ladders may occupy the dedicated space above the gear if the front stays clear
Required working space cannot be used for storage, and combustibles stay out
A locked electrical room waives the NEC 110.26 working-space clearance rules

explanation: NEC 110.26(B) forbids using required working space for storage. Combustibles next to switchgear add fire load and block emergency access. Dedicated equipment space above gear must also stay clear. Locking the room does not reduce the clearance dimensions.

distractorExplanations.a: A leftover walkway does not satisfy 110.26 depth and width; the working space itself cannot be storage.
distractorExplanations.b: 110.26(E) dedicated space above equipment is for raceways and ventilation, not ladder or material storage.
distractorExplanations.d: Access control does not waive working space; clearances apply whether or not the door is locked.

prompt: After LOTO on a 480 V motor disconnect, the journeyman must prove the load side is dead before lifting motor leads. What method is required?

options.text: Sweep a non-contact tester near each conductor and stop if the wand is silent
Open the breaker and rely on the panel schedule as the official dead check
Measure one phase-to-ground pair and treat the remaining phases as matching
Use a rated contact tester on each phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground pair

explanation: NFPA 70E requires an adequately rated contact instrument. Test phase-to-phase and phase-to-ground on every conductor, using live-dead-live to prove the meter. Non-contact wands, schedules, and a single pair can miss a still-live lead on a motor circuit.

distractorExplanations.a: Non-contact testers can miss shielded or low voltage and are not the accepted absence-of-voltage method.
distractorExplanations.b: Panel schedules are often wrong; documentation is not a voltage test.
distractorExplanations.c: One phase-to-ground reading can miss an open ground or a live remaining phase; all combinations are required.

prompt: A 480 V MCC bucket must be racked. Under NEC Article 100, who is a qualified person for that task?

options.text: Any state-licensed journeyman, even when untrained on this specific MCC
A person skilled on this equipment and trained to recognize and avoid its hazards
Anyone who finished OSHA 10 awareness training, without equipment-specific practice
An operator who has run the production line for years without electrical safety training

explanation: Article 100 defines a qualified person as one with skills and knowledge related to the construction and operation of the electrical equipment and who has received safety training to recognize and avoid the hazards involved. A license, OSHA 10, or operating experience without that training does not meet the definition.

distractorExplanations.a: A license is not the Article 100 test; qualification is equipment- and hazard-specific skills plus safety training.
distractorExplanations.c: OSHA 10 is general awareness; racking an MCC requires training on that gear and its shock and arc-flash hazards.
distractorExplanations.d: Years of operation without electrical hazard training leave the person unqualified for exposed 480 V work.

prompt: A motor nameplate shows 24 A full-load current and a service factor of 1.15. Under NEC 430.32(A)(1), what is the maximum setting of the separate overload device?

options.text: 125% of a table full-load current used in place of the nameplate amperes
30 A, from 125% of the 24 A nameplate full-load current
27.6 A, from 115% of the 24 A nameplate full-load current
60 A, from the 250% inverse-time breaker percentage on the nameplate

explanation: NEC 430.32(A)(1) limits a separate overload device to 125% of the motor nameplate full-load current when the marked service factor is 1.15 or greater. The nameplate current is 24 A, and 24 × 1.25 = 30 A, which is that maximum. A table full-load current, the 115% nameplate row, and a short-circuit breaker percentage are different rules.

distractorExplanations.a: 430.32 sizes this overload from nameplate full-load amperes. Substituting a Table 430.250 full-load current uses the wrong current.
distractorExplanations.c: 27.6 A is 115% of 24 A. That row is for a service factor below 1.15 with no 40°C rise mark, so it is not the maximum for this 1.15 service factor.
distractorExplanations.d: 60 A applies the 250% inverse-time breaker percentage for a Design B squirrel-cage motor. That Table 430.52 value is short-circuit protection, not the overload setting.

prompt: A rooftop condenser fan is marked 20 A full-load. Its service factor is 1.00, and the nameplate is silent on temperature rise. The separate overload heaters are being ordered. What maximum does 430.32(A)(1) allow?

options.text: 23 A, from 115% of the 20 A nameplate full-load current
25 A, from 125% of the 20 A nameplate full-load current
A table full-load current used in place of the 20 A nameplate full-load current
50 A, from the 250% inverse-time breaker percentage on the nameplate

explanation: NEC 430.32(A)(1) limits the separate overload to 115% of nameplate full-load current when the service factor is 1.0 and the nameplate has no 40°C rise mark. This motor is marked 20 A, so the maximum is 20 × 1.15 = 23 A. The 125% nameplate figure exceeds that maximum, and a table full-load current or a short-circuit percentage does not set this overload.

distractorExplanations.b: 25 A is 125% of the 20 A nameplate. That percentage needs a service factor of 1.15 or greater, or a 40°C rise mark, which this nameplate does not have.
distractorExplanations.c: A separate overload device under 430.32 is based on the nameplate full-load current, not on a Table 430.250 full-load current.
distractorExplanations.d: 50 A applies the 250% inverse-time breaker percentage used for a Design B squirrel-cage motor. That is short-circuit protection, not this overload setting.

prompt: A single continuous-duty motor has a nameplate current of 14 A and a table full-load current of 17 A. What minimum conductor ampacity do NEC 430.22 and 430.6 require for the branch circuit?

options.text: 17.5 A, from 125% of the 14 A nameplate instead of the table full-load current
17 A, the table full-load current with the 125% multiplier left off
21.25 A, from 125% of the 17 A table full-load current
14 A only, taken from the nameplate and leaving out both the table current and the 125% factor

explanation: NEC 430.6 requires these branch-circuit conductors to be sized from the table full-load current, not the nameplate. NEC 430.22 then requires 125% of that table value for a single continuous-duty motor. The table current is 17 A, so 17 × 1.25 = 21.25 A.

distractorExplanations.a: 17.5 A multiplies the 14 A nameplate by 125%. These conductors use the table full-load current, which is 17 A, not the nameplate.
distractorExplanations.b: 17 A is the table full-load current with the 125% factor omitted. 430.22 requires that multiplier for this single continuous-duty motor.
distractorExplanations.d: 14 A is the nameplate alone. 430.6 does not let the nameplate replace the table value when the branch conductors are sized.

prompt: A Design B squirrel-cage motor has a table full-load current of 20 A, and 50 A is a standard rating. The branch-circuit short-circuit device is an inverse-time breaker. What maximum rating does Table 430.52 permit?

options.text: A 35 A dual-element time-delay fuse taken from the 175% fuse column
A 160 A instantaneous-trip breaker using the 800% instantaneous-trip percentage on this motor
An overload device set at 115% of the 20 A table full-load current
A 50 A inverse-time breaker, at 250% of the table full-load current

explanation: Table 430.52 lists 250% of full-load current for an inverse-time breaker on a Design B squirrel-cage motor. The table full-load current is 20 A, and 20 × 2.50 = 50 A, which is a standard rating, so that is the maximum. The dual-element fuse column, an instantaneous-trip breaker, and an overload percentage are not this inverse-time breaker.

distractorExplanations.a: 35 A is 175% of 20 A, the dual-element time-delay fuse percentage. The inverse-time breaker column for this Design B motor is 250%, which is 50 A.
distractorExplanations.b: 160 A is 800% of 20 A, an instantaneous-trip figure. This question asks for the inverse-time breaker, which Table 430.52 sets at 250%, or 50 A.
distractorExplanations.c: 115% is an overload percentage. Table 430.52 selects the short-circuit and ground-fault device, not the overload relay.

prompt: A Design B squirrel-cage motor has a table full-load current of 20 A. The branch-circuit short-circuit device is a dual-element time-delay fuse. What maximum rating does Table 430.52 permit?

options.text: A 50 A inverse-time breaker taken from the 250% breaker column instead of the fuse column
A 35 A dual-element time-delay fuse, at 175% of the table full-load current
A 160 A instantaneous-trip breaker applying the 800% instantaneous-trip percentage to the 20 A table current
An overload device held at 115% of the 20 A table full-load current and used as the fuse

explanation: Table 430.52 lists 175% of full-load current for a dual-element time-delay fuse on a Design B squirrel-cage motor. The table full-load current is 20 A, and 20 × 1.75 = 35 A, which is the maximum fuse rating. That fuse column is separate from the 250% inverse-time breaker column, an instantaneous-trip figure, and the overload rule.

distractorExplanations.a: 50 A is 250% of 20 A, the inverse-time breaker percentage for a Design B squirrel-cage motor. The device asked for here is the dual-element fuse at 175%.
distractorExplanations.c: 160 A is 800% of 20 A, an instantaneous-trip figure. It is not the dual-element time-delay fuse, which Table 430.52 sets at 175%, or 35 A.
distractorExplanations.d: 115% of table current is an overload setting. It does not select the dual-element time-delay fuse under Table 430.52.

prompt: Three motors that are not continuous loads share one feeder. Their table full-load currents are 20 A, 10 A, and 8 A. NEC 430.24 still requires 125% of the largest motor plus the full-load current of the other motors. What minimum feeder conductor ampacity is required?

options.text: 43 A, from 125% of the 20 A motor plus the 10 A and 8 A motors
47.5 A, from 125% of the sum of the 20 A, 10 A, and 8 A table currents
38 A, the plain sum of the 20 A, 10 A, and 8 A table currents with no 125% factor
42.5 A, from 100% of the 20 A motor plus 125% of the 10 A and 8 A motors

explanation: NEC 430.24 sizes the feeder at 125% of the largest motor's table full-load current plus the other motors at 100%, and that largest-motor factor stays even when the motors are not continuous loads. The largest is 20 A, so 20 × 1.25 = 25 A, then 25 + 10 + 8 = 43 A. The 125% factor is not applied to the whole sum, and it is not moved onto the smaller motors.

distractorExplanations.b: 125% of the whole sum is 47.5 A. 430.24 applies 125% only to the largest motor, then adds the 10 A and 8 A motors at their table current.
distractorExplanations.c: 38 A adds 20 A, 10 A, and 8 A with no 125% factor. The largest motor still has to be taken at 125%, which is 25 A, before the others are added.
distractorExplanations.d: 42.5 A puts 125% on the 10 A and 8 A motors and leaves the 20 A motor at 100%. 430.24 puts the 125% factor on the largest motor only.

prompt: From the motor, the disconnect is visible across an open floor, and the handle is 70 ft away. For the disconnect required by NEC 430.102, is that disconnect in sight from the motor?

options.text: Yes. The disconnect is visible, so the 70 ft distance still counts as in sight
Yes. A lockable disconnect is treated as in sight at any distance when the motor can be seen from the handle
No. It is not in sight, because in sight also means not more than 50 ft
No. The disconnect has to be mounted on the motor itself before 430.102 treats it as in sight

explanation: Article 100 defines in sight as visible and not more than 50 ft apart. A disconnect that can be seen from the motor but stands 70 ft away fails that definition, so it is not the in-sight motor disconnect required by NEC 430.102. Visibility alone, or a lockable handle, does not stretch the 50 ft limit.

distractorExplanations.a: Visibility is only half of the definition. At 70 ft the disconnect is past the 50 ft limit, so it is not in sight from the motor.
distractorExplanations.b: A lockable open position is a separate feature of the disconnect. It does not waive the 50 ft limit inside the definition of in sight.
distractorExplanations.d: 430.102 does not require the disconnect to be mounted on the motor. This one fails because 70 ft is more than the 50 ft in-sight limit.

prompt: A controller is being ordered for a 5 hp motor, and NEC 430.83 is the selection rule. Which controller meets that rule?

options.text: Any 20 A general-use snap switch, with no horsepower rating required for this 5 hp motor
A switch chosen only by matching its ampere rating to the motor nameplate current
No separate controller, because the overload relay replaces the controller
A controller with a horsepower rating not less than this 5 hp motor

explanation: NEC 430.83 requires a motor controller to have a horsepower rating not less than the horsepower rating of the motor. A controller for this 5 hp motor must be rated at least 5 hp. A 20 A general-use snap switch, a switch picked only from nameplate amperes, and the overload relay do not meet that horsepower rule.

distractorExplanations.a: The general-use snap switch allowance is for a stationary motor of 2 hp or less, not this 5 hp motor. 430.83 still requires a horsepower rating at least equal to the motor.
distractorExplanations.b: Matching a switch to nameplate amperes skips the horsepower rating that 430.83 requires. An ampere match alone does not satisfy the controller rule.
distractorExplanations.c: The overload relay protects against overload current. It does not replace the controller that starts and stops the motor.

prompt: A helper holds a disconnect handle in the off position while another electrician works on the circuit. No lock is on the handle. Why is that not lockout?

options.text: It would count as lockout if the helper kept a hand on the handle until the work was finished
A held handle is not a lock; each exposed person applies their own lock
A tag on the handle is the lockout by itself, so the helper's hand is only extra
The helper at the handle covers the other worker, so that second person does not apply a lock

explanation: Lockout means each person who could be exposed applies a personal lock at the isolation point. A helper holding the handle can be called away, and nothing then keeps the disconnect from being closed. A hand on the handle, a tag, or one person's presence in place of the other person's lock does not lock out every exposed person.

distractorExplanations.a: A hand on the handle is not a lock. If the helper lets go, the disconnect can be closed on the people who are still exposed.
distractorExplanations.c: A tag is not a personal lock. Each person who could be exposed has to apply that person's own lock, not rely on a tag.
distractorExplanations.d: One person standing at the handle does not cover the other exposed worker. Each person who could be exposed applies a separate lock.

prompt: A Design B squirrel-cage motor has a table full-load current of 14 A, and the branch conductors are 12 AWG copper. Table 430.52 puts the inverse-time breaker at 250% of that table current, which is 35 A. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The breaker must be 20 A, because NEC 240.4(D) is what sets the short-circuit device on this 12 AWG motor branch
The inverse-time breaker stays at 35 A; 40 A is not permitted as the next size
The 12 AWG copper is too small for a conductor ampacity of 14 A times 125% and has to be replaced first
The overload device must be removed so the breaker above 35 A becomes the only motor protection

explanation: Table 430.52 sets this Design B inverse-time breaker at 250% of the 14 A table full-load current, which is 35 A. 35 A is already a standard rating, so the next-size permission does not raise it to 40 A. The conductors need 14 × 1.25 = 17.5 A, and 12 AWG copper covers that. NEC 240.4(G) places this motor short-circuit device under Article 430, so 240.4(D) does not set it, and the overload device stays.

distractorExplanations.a: 240.4(D) would hold an ordinary 12 AWG conductor to a 20 A device, but 240.4(G) sends this motor short-circuit device to Article 430 instead.
distractorExplanations.c: The branch conductors need 14 × 1.25 = 17.5 A. 12 AWG copper is large enough for that ampacity, so it does not have to be replaced.
distractorExplanations.d: The overload device is still required. Leaving the inverse-time breaker at 35 A does not mean the overload relay is removed.

prompt: A label on the equipment states an arc-flash boundary of 4 ft and a restricted approach boundary of 1 ft. What do those two labeled boundaries represent?

options.text: Both labeled distances are shock boundaries, and the 4 ft figure is the working clearance left open in front of this equipment
Both labeled distances are thermal boundaries, and the 1 ft figure is the point where bare-hand contact with the equipment becomes allowed
The restricted approach boundary is the shock boundary, and the arc-flash boundary is the thermal boundary
The arc-flash boundary is the shock boundary, and the restricted approach boundary is the thermal boundary on this label

explanation: The label gives a restricted approach boundary of 1 ft and an arc-flash boundary of 4 ft. The restricted approach boundary is the shock boundary, so crossing it is a shock-protection decision. The arc-flash boundary is the thermal boundary. Treating both distances as the same kind of boundary, or swapping the two roles, misreads the label.

distractorExplanations.a: The two figures are not both shock boundaries. The restricted approach boundary is the shock boundary, and the arc-flash boundary is the thermal boundary.
distractorExplanations.b: The two figures are not both thermal boundaries. The 1 ft restricted approach boundary is a shock boundary, not a bare-hand thermal limit.
distractorExplanations.d: This swaps the two boundaries. On the label, the 4 ft arc-flash boundary is thermal and the 1 ft restricted approach boundary is the shock boundary.

prompt: A task needs shock protection for a 480 V phase-to-phase exposure. ASTM rates Class 00 rubber gloves at 500 V AC and Class 0 rubber gloves at 1000 V AC. This 480 V system can operate above that 500 V Class 00 maximum. Which glove selection is required?

options.text: Class 00, because 480 V phase-to-phase sits under the 500 V AC maximum of that class
Leather protector gloves worn alone, with no rubber insulating gloves under them
Class 00 selected from 277 V to ground rather than from the 480 V phase-to-phase exposure
Class 0 or a higher class for this 480 V exposure, not Class 00

explanation: Class 00 rubber insulating gloves have a maximum use voltage of 500 V AC, and Class 0 gloves are rated 1000 V AC. A 480 V nominal system can operate above that 500 V Class 00 limit, so this phase-to-phase exposure needs Class 0 or a higher class. Leather protectors are worn over rubber gloves and do not take their place, and 277 V to ground is not the exposure given here.

distractorExplanations.a: Class 00 stops at 500 V AC. Treating 480 V as automatically under that ceiling misses that this system can operate above 500 V, so the gloves need to be Class 0 or higher.
distractorExplanations.b: Leather protectors do not insulate. They are worn over rubber insulating gloves and are not a substitute for Class 0 or higher.
distractorExplanations.c: 277 V to ground is not the exposure in the stem. The glove has to match the 480 V phase-to-phase shock protection, which is Class 0 or higher.

prompt: A column beside the hinge side stops a panelboard door at 45 degrees. The space in front of the panel is otherwise clear. Does NEC 110.26 permit that door?

options.text: Not permitted. Equipment doors must open at least 90 degrees
Permitted, because the working space in front of the panel is already clear and that is the only door rule in 110.26
Permitted when the deadfront can still be taken off with tools while the door sits stopped at 45 degrees
Permitted, because a building column beside the hinge side is an allowed reason for the door to stop short of 90 degrees

explanation: NEC 110.26 requires the working space to let equipment doors and hinged panels open at least 90 degrees. A door that a column stops at 45 degrees does not meet that rule, even when the floor in front of the panel is clear. Removing a cover with tools, or blaming the column, does not replace the 90-degree opening.

distractorExplanations.b: A clear floor does not cure the door. 110.26 still requires the equipment door to open at least 90 degrees, and this door stops at 45.
distractorExplanations.c: Being able to unbolt a deadfront is not the rule being applied. The hinged door itself must open at least 90 degrees.
distractorExplanations.d: A column beside the hinge is the reason the door fails. 110.26 does not waive the 90-degree opening because the building is in the way.

prompt: A three-phase motor was running under load. The overload device then tripped, and one ungrounded conductor is found open. What does that condition show?

options.text: Any overload trip means the heater is too small and has to be replaced with a larger heater
A GFCI is the device that would see this open conductor, so the trip was a ground-fault trip
The overload should come out and the breaker should be raised so the motor can run on the remaining conductors
The motor was single-phasing, and the overload device did its job

explanation: An open ungrounded conductor on a running three-phase motor leaves the motor single-phasing. Current in the remaining conductors rises, and the overload device is there to open. This trip means the overload did its job. It does not by itself prove the heater is too small, it is not a GFCI function, and taking the overload out would leave the single-phasing motor unprotected.

distractorExplanations.a: An overload trip does not automatically mean the heater is too small. An open conductor caused single-phasing, and the overload opened as it should.
distractorExplanations.b: A GFCI looks for a small current imbalance. An overload relay opening on single-phasing current is not a ground-fault trip.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the overload and raising the breaker leaves the single-phasing motor without the device that just took it offline.

prompt: A motor disconnect is open. Another source can backfeed the motor leads. Before those leads are lifted, how does the journeyman treat the conductors?

options.text: An open local disconnect guarantees that the motor leads have no voltage left from any source
Prove the conductors dead, because another source can backfeed them
A helper watching the disconnect handle is enough to show that a second source cannot backfeed the leads
The motor nameplate voltage is used in place of a test once the local disconnect has been opened

explanation: Opening the local disconnect does not prove the motor leads are dead when another source can backfeed them. The journeyman treats those conductors as energized until a test proves them dead. A helper watching the handle, the open disconnect by itself, and the nameplate voltage are not that proof.

distractorExplanations.a: An open local disconnect does not guarantee zero voltage on the leads when another source can backfeed the motor circuit.
distractorExplanations.c: A helper watching the handle cannot detect a backfeed from another source. Watching the handle is not a test that the conductors are dead.
distractorExplanations.d: The nameplate states the motor rating. It does not prove the conductors are dead before the leads are lifted.
